nameStory: This lichen gets its "antler" name from its branching, finger-like lobes that spread out like a deer's antlers. The word "common" simply means it's one of the more frequently spotted antler lichens in our region, though with only 71 recorded observations in New England, it's still a special find!
description: Common Antler Lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms spreading patches on tree bark and rocks. It grows in flattened, branching lobes that create an antler-like pattern, typically reaching 2-4 inches across. The lichen has a distinctive two-toned appearance with different colors on top and bottom surfaces. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as a team.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for numerous small, finger-like bumps called isidia scattered across the upper surface - these feel slightly rougher than the surrounding lichen and are key identification features

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flattened, branching lobes that spread outward like antlers or fingers, creating distinctive radiating patterns

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface is typically grayish-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet, while the underside is usually much paler or whitish

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and somewhat papery when dry, but becomes softer and more pliable when moistened by rain or dew

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes are relatively narrow compared to other antler lichens, typically less than half an inch wide

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Usually grows on tree bark, particularly favoring hardwood trees, but can also be found on rocks in suitable conditions

habitat: Common Antler Lichen grows primarily on the bark of deciduous trees in New England's forests, particularly favoring maple, oak, and birch trees. You'll often find it in somewhat open woodlands or forest edges where there's good air circulation but not too much direct sunlight. It can occasionally be spotted on rocks, especially in areas with consistent moisture and moderate shade.

seasonality.spring: Fresh spring rains bring out the lichen's most vibrant green colors, making it easier to spot against tree bark. The increased moisture makes the surface feel soft and pliable to gentle touch.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen appears more grayish and feels papery or brittle. Look for the characteristic isidia bumps which remain visible even when the lichen is drought-stressed.
seasonality.fall: Autumn's frequent rains rehydrate the lichen, restoring its green tones. This is an excellent time for identification as the lichen contrasts nicely with colorful fall foliage.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable on bare tree trunks, though colors may be muted. Snow and ice can temporarily obscure specimens, but they remain present year-round on their host trees.

funFact: The tiny bumps (isidia) on this lichen are actually living "baby lichens" ready to break off and start new colonies - it's like the lichen is covered in its own children, just waiting for the right wind or raindrop to carry them to a new home!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other antler-like lichens, but Common Antler Lichen's numerous isidia (small bumps) and relatively narrow lobes help distinguish it. Memory trick: "Common has lots of bumps in common" - if you see many small bumps across the surface, you're likely looking at Common Antler Lichen rather than its smoother relatives.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Pseudevernia means "false Evernia," referring to its similarity to another genus of lichens. This reflects how lichen classification has evolved as scientists better understand these complex partnerships between fungi and algae.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Light-and-dark Lichen (Pseudevernia cladonia), Common Antler Lichen has much more abundant isidia and narrower lobes. Light-and-dark Lichen tends to have broader, more contrasting colored lobes with fewer reproductive bumps. If you see lots of small bumps and narrow branching, you're likely looking at Common Antler Lichen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Light-and-dark Lichen differs from its close relative Common Antler Lichen primarily in growth form and habitat - while both may show color variations, Common Antler Lichen grows in more three-dimensional, branched structures rather than the flat, leafy patches of Light-and-dark Lichen.
